text: Chapter 2 introduced anomaly-based detection — flagging traffic that deviates from what's normal, instead of matching known-bad signatures. That raises an obvious question: normal according to what? The answer is a traffic baseline, a recorded profile built from flow data collected over days or weeks, covering how much a host typically sends, who it typically talks to, and when it's typically active.

A baseline isn't a single number — it's three dimensions at once. Volume is how much traffic a host moves and how that varies hour to hour. Destinations are the IPs, ports, and regions it routinely contacts, versus ones it's never touched. Timing is when it's normally active, since a workstation idle every night between 11 PM and 6 AM has a timing baseline just as real as its volume baseline.

Take a finance department workstation with a well-established baseline: a handful of internal IPs, active only 8 AM to 6 PM, never moving more than a few hundred megabytes a day. At 3 AM, flow data shows it opening a large outbound connection to a country it's never contacted. No signature matched anything — but it breaks all three dimensions of the baseline at once, exactly the combination anomaly-based detection is built to catch.

That baseline only means something relative to the host it describes. A backup server moving tens of gigabytes to a storage array at 2 AM is completely normal for that server; a user workstation doing the same thing at 2 AM almost certainly isn't. That's why baselining has to be scoped per host or per segment type — a single network-wide average would blur those legitimate differences together and miss what matters.

Without a baseline, anomaly-based detection has nothing to compare against — it's the missing piece that makes Chapter 2's approach actually work in practice. Next up: putting baselining and flow data to work against a specific threat, data exfiltration, and the traffic patterns that give it away.
